item.title: Exclusive: How Sen. Schatz is talking about climate in an affordability crisis
item.description:
Source: Axios Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Americans are "connecting the dots" between climate and affordability strain, Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) said Monday at an Axios House event on the sidelines of Climate Week and the UN General Assembly. Why it matters: But as pocketbook issues dominate a critical midterm race, Schatz says that doesn't mean the first thing he mentions to constituents is climate. Still, climate-tangent conversations — like utility prices and the data center boom — are looming over the polls. Driving the news: "I think we should talk about climate in the context of people not being able to afford their lives," Schatz told Axios' Ben Geman, pointing to insurance non-renewals, soaring gas prices and rising utility bills . "It's not that difficult anymore for us to be able to say, look, one of the reasons things are getting more expensive is we're not addressing the climate crisis," he said, criticizing the federal government's renewables roadblocks. "The climate imperatives used to have to be balanced against people's pocketbooks, and now they are perfectly lined up," he added. "We do not have to make trade-offs. They are deciding to make the planet worse and make your pocketbook situation worse." Catch up quick: Schatz has been a leading congressional voice on climate issues, representing a heavily petroleum -dependent U.S. state with high energy prices that's at particular risk from the impacts of climate change. The state has taken on an ambitious clean energy initiative that aims for 100% renewable energy by 2035 on the neighbor islands, including Maui and Hawaiʻi. Friction point: The sweeping GOP budget bill signed into law by President Trump last year phased out wind, solar, and electric vehicle subsidies that the prior administration championed as tools to bolster clean tech. It's one front in Trump's broader rollback of Biden-era climate policies , including moves to kill regulations and a slowdown in permitting of renewables projects. In particular, administration officials have targeted wind power, which Trump has repeatedly criticized. Still, the AI boom is expected to drive a surge in clean energy this year. Go deeper: New signs Iran war is boosting clean energy

item.title: The Trouble With the Nuclear-AI Analogy
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Pre-analysis score: 0.84
In humanity’s quest to constrain the dangers from fast-advancing artificial intelligence, many have looked to the most revolutionary technology that preceded it: nuclear weapons. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has called artificial intelligence “far more dangerous than nukes.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who assigns The Making of the Atomic Bomb to employees and has likened himself to the Manhattan Project scientist Leo Szilard, describes the most powerful AI models as “weaponizable nuclear materials.” When asked how a technology such as AI can be regulated, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman often references the world’s nuclear materials watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency. Even the director of the CIA, John Ratcliffe, has made the same comparison.These comparisons capture real parallels. Like nuclear weapons, frontier AI is powerful and hard to control. Like nuclear technology, it can be used for good or for ill. And like the Cold War arms race, the race for AI breakthroughs may reorder the global balance of power. The nuclear analogy, then, seems to offer a blueprint for how to effectively govern a promising but potentially dangerous technology such as AI.
